subject: biology
title: Surface area to volume ratio and exchange surfaces
key_idea: As an organism gets larger, its surface area to volume ratio falls. Small organisms can exchange substances across their surface alone. Larger organisms need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems.

blocks.text: This section covers how size changes the ratio, and why it matters for exchange.

diagram.alt: Change the side of a cube and watch the surface area to volume ratio

items.text: Surface area is 6 × 1 × 1 = 6 cm². Volume is 1 cm³. The ratio is 6 : 1.
Surface area is 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cm². Volume is 8 cm³. The ratio is 3 : 1.
Surface area is 6 × 4 × 4 = 96 cm². Volume is 64 cm³. The ratio is 1.5 : 1.

items: Volume increases faster than surface area as size increases, so the ratio falls.
Surface area is the area through which substances enter and leave.
Volume is the amount of living tissue that needs supplying and that produces waste.
SA:V is surface area divided by volume.
The ratio decreases as size increases.
Larger organisms have less surface per unit of volume.

blocks.text: Organisms exchange gases, nutrients and waste with their surroundings. How they do it depends on their SA:V ratio and their metabolic rate.

rows: Short, so substances reach the centre quickly
Long, so diffusion alone is too slow
Specialised exchange surfaces, such as lungs, and a transport system

items: A high metabolic rate means a high demand for oxygen and a lot of heat produced.
Small mammals have a large SA:V ratio, so they lose heat quickly. They need a high metabolic rate to stay warm.
Larger animals have a smaller ratio, so they lose less heat per unit of body volume.
Changes in body shape can reduce the loss of heat, such as small ears and a rounded body in cold climates, and large ears in hot ones.
Small organisms can exchange across their surface because the ratio is large.
Large organisms need exchange surfaces and transport systems.
SA:V links to metabolic rate and to heat loss.

sections.heading: Features of an efficient exchange surface

blocks.text: Exchange surfaces are adapted to make diffusion fast.

rows: More room for particles to cross
Root hair cells, villi and alveoli
Alveoli walls are one cell thick
Carries substances away, so the concentration gradient is kept steep
Capillaries around alveoli, and gill lamellae
Brings in fresh air or water, so the gradient is maintained
Breathing in the lungs, and water flow over gills

items: An efficient surface is large, thin and kept at a steep gradient.
Blood flow and ventilation maintain the gradient.

blocks.text: Agar blocks containing an indicator model cells of different size.

items.text: Cut agar blocks of different sizes, such as cubes of 1, 2 and 3 cm sides. The agar contains an indicator.
Place the blocks in acid or alkali at the same time, so the indicator changes colour as the substance diffuses in.
Record how long each block takes to change colour all the way through.
Work out the SA:V of each block and compare it with the time taken.

items: Smaller blocks have a larger SA:V and change colour all the way through more quickly.
A larger block has a longer distance to the centre, and a smaller area for each unit of volume.
Control temperature and concentration, and use the same cutting method.
Higher SA:V gives faster diffusion to the centre.
Time to change colour measures the effect.

checks.q: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 3 cm.
checks.a: Surface area = 6 × 3 × 3 = 54 cm². Volume = 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cm³. Ratio = 54 ÷ 27 = 2 : 1.

checks.q: Explain why a large multicellular organism needs a specialised gas exchange surface, but an amoeba does not.
checks.a: The amoeba has a large SA:V ratio and a short diffusion distance, so oxygen can diffuse across its surface fast enough. The multicellular organism has a small SA:V ratio and a long diffusion distance, so diffusion across the body surface is too slow.

checks.q: Give three features of an efficient exchange surface.
checks.a: Any three from: large surface area, thin layer or short diffusion distance, good blood supply, ventilation, and a steep concentration gradient.

items: Relate the SA:V ratio to metabolic rate.
Changes to body shape and the development of systems in larger organisms are adaptations that facilitate exchange as the ratio decreases.
Calculate the surface areas and volumes of simple 3-D shapes to show that SA:V decreases with size.
Investigate the effect of changing SA:V on diffusion using agar blocks of different sizes.
Link the need for exchange surfaces to SA:V, metabolic activity, and single-celled and multicellular organisms.
Examples of efficient features: increased surface area in root hair cells, a thin layer in alveoli, and good blood supply or ventilation to maintain the gradient in gills and alveoli.
